title: Put on mercy (Colossians 3:12–17)
hookLine: put on mercy, kindness, humility, and above all charity

lines: CLOTHES THAT CHANGE HOW YOU STAND.
TAKE OFF THE OLD, PUT ON THE NEW.
cards: Some clothes change how you stand. A uniform on the first day of a job. A borrowed suit at a funeral.
The jersey of your team on game day. Paul writes to Colossae, a small town in what's now Turkey, to a church he seems never to have visited. And in the third chapter he talks about getting dressed.
First, take off the old self like a worn-out coat: anger, malice, lying. Then, he says, here is what to put on.

teach.h: BOWELS OF MERCY: FELT IN THE GUT.
teach.b: In the Douay-Rheims: "Put ye on therefore, as the elect of God, holy, and beloved, the bowels of mercy, benignity, humility, modesty, patience." Bowels of mercy sounds strange, but it's honest about the body.
The Greek word means the inner organs, the gut, where people of that time felt compassion. We'd say heart.
Then the five garments: mercy, kindness, humility, gentleness, patience.

And what they're for: "Bearing with one another, and forgiving one another, if any have a complaint against another: even as the Lord hath forgiven you, so do you also." Paul doesn't pretend there will be no complaints.
He assumes there will be, and tells them what to wear when it happens.

teach.h: CHARITY: THE BOND THAT HOLDS IT ALL.
teach.b: Then the last piece: "But above all these things have charity, which is the bond of perfection." Bond is the word we met in Ephesians: syndesmos, the binding.
A chapter earlier Paul used it for the bands that hold a body together.

teach.h: ABOVE ALL THESE THINGS HAVE CHARITY.
teach.b: Charity holds the other virtues together. Without it, they come apart.

Then the chapter widens: let the peace of Christ rule in your hearts, let the word of Christ dwell in you richly, singing psalms and hymns, and whatever you do, in word or in deed, do all in the name of the Lord Jesus, giving thanks.
Catholic priests have an old custom that puts this on the body.
For centuries, as a priest put on each vestment before Mass, he said a short prayer for a matching virtue: purity with the cincture tied at the waist, for one.
The prayers are now optional, but some priests still say them.

how: Traditionally, a priest says a short vesting prayer as he puts on each vestment before Mass; the prayers are optional today but still used by some, and many Catholics pray a morning offering at the start of the day.

o: the bond that holds a body, or virtues, together
the Greek word for a list of five virtues
a vestment a priest ties around his waist

games.q: the new clothes — tap the pairs.

s: Paul founded the church at Colossae himself
the letter names Epaphras as their teacher (1:7) and suggests Paul had never visited (2:1).
Paul expects there to be complaints among them
"if any have a complaint against another": forgive, as the Lord forgave you.
the Greek really means inner organs, where people felt compassion.

games.q: someone in your church has a real complaint against you. what does Paul tell the Colossians to wear for it?
o: mercy, patience, and forgiveness, as the Lord forgave you.
the right to be proven right.
games.why: "bearing with one another, and forgiving one another... even as the Lord hath forgiven you, so do you also."

practice: Think of the person most likely to bring you a complaint today, or to get one from you.
Of the five, mercy, kindness, humility, gentleness or patience, choose the one you'd most need with them, and give that word to the last thing you'll put on before you go out.
If you pray, say Paul's line as you touch it, above all these things have charity; if not, let the cloth carry the word.

wordCard.voice: Syndesmos, the binding. The word Paul uses for charity, which holds together mercy, kindness, humility, gentleness and patience. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: the inner organs, the seat of compassion; 'bowels of mercy' (Colossians 3:12).

carryVoice: Your line: above all, charity. The bond that keeps the rest from coming apart. Day five hundred ninety-two, in the books.
